feat(server): report the version, and stop announcing a socket that does not exist yet (#90) (#72)

There was no way to ask a running node what version it is. Not `--print-config`,
not `STATUS`, not `/metrics`. The only occurrence of the version anywhere in the
C++ was a hardcoded literal in `tools/ob_tcp_server.cpp`. For a database an
evaluator is deciding whether to trust, "which build is this node running" was a
question with no answer.

Found while writing the comparative harness for #39, which records the version of
every system it measures beside the numbers. It can read ClickHouse's from
`SELECT version()` and ours from nothing, so its results file said "unreported
(the server has no way to report its version)" — the honest artefact, and the
argument for this change.

**The banner lied twice.** It ran *before* the `TcpServer` was constructed, so
`listening on port N` announced a socket that did not exist yet; a bind that then
failed for a taken port left the output claiming to listen with the error
underneath it. And it went to `stdout` through `printf` with no flush, which is
block-buffered whenever stdout is not a terminal — so redirected to a file, a
pipe or a journal, the one line an operator greps to confirm a start arrived at
**process exit**. Every JSON line was on time because the logger writes to
unbuffered `stderr`. Measured: absent from a node's log file while the node was
up and answering.

Now: the version comes from `project(... VERSION)` through a compile definition,
so the C++ has one copy and `ob::version()` is the only way to get it. The
startup line says **starting** and is flushed. The line reporting a working
socket is logged by the server after the bind and the listen have both succeeded.
And the version is askable three ways — `STATUS` gains a `version:` key/value
line, not a column, so no client parsing the tab-separated table has to change;
and `/metrics` gains `ob_build_info{version="…",node_role="…"} 1`, the
conventional shape, which is what lets a monitoring system tell an old binary
from a new one across a fleet.

Verified by starting a node and asking it, rather than by reading: the banner is
in the redirected file while the node is up, the logger's `listening on port …,
version 0.1.0` line is there, `STATUS` answers `version: 0.1.0`, and `/metrics`
answers `ob_build_info{version="0.1.0",node_role="standalone"} 1`.

**Two drift guards, both mutation-checked.** `pyproject.toml` still carries its
own version, because a wheel's metadata cannot be a C++ macro — one test holds
the two in step, and another refuses the version as a literal in any of the four
sources that report it. A literal that agrees today drifts at the first bump, and
the symptom is an operator told the wrong build is running, which is worse than
being told nothing.

`docs/operations.md` gains the three ways to ask, and why the startup line says
"starting" rather than "listening".

fix(mcp): default-bind to 0.0.0.0 + expose 8502 — LAN MCP works out of the box

PR #398 (commits on next via the MCP security hardening series) flipped
the default to 127.0.0.1 and commented out the port mapping, citing a
deliberate opt-in policy. In practice arkiv's deployment model is one
machine runs arkiv, the rest of the LAN connects via MCP clients — every
fresh docker compose up hit the same problem (port 8502 reachable on
nothing), and the documented opt-in steps in README were easy to miss.

The token gate is the real security boundary, not the bind address: the
server is read-only, every request needs Authorization: Bearer <token>,
and the token store is shared with the main HTTP API. Loopback-bind added
friction without adding meaningful security for the LAN-host case.

This commit:
- flips ARKIV_MCP_BIND default in mcp_http_server.py to 0.0.0.0
- sets the env to 0.0.0.0 and uncomments the ports: 8502:8502 mapping
  in docker-compose.yml
- rewrites the arkiv-mcp comment block in docker-compose.yml to document
  the new default and the opt-out path
- updates mcp_http_server.py docstring to match
- rewrites the Exposing MCP to LAN section in README.md: documents the
  new default + security model, and adds Locking MCP down to localhost
  steps for users who want the old opt-in behavior

Preserved from the MCP security hardening series:
- ?token= query-param auth is still rejected (Bearer-only)
- DNS rebinding protection in mcp_server.py is still disabled
- The public-internet-exposure warnings are still in place

subscriptions.last_commit_message:
policy: every operation asks the engine, once, at its entry point

53 gate calls across eleven modules of antares-api, one per NGSI-LD
operation and each naming its clause. AppState carries the engine
(AllowAll unless a host replaces it with with_policy); a refusal is
403 with this broker's own urn:antares:error:AccessDenied, since
Table 6.3.2-1 names no access-denied error. antares-broker picks the
engine off POLICY_SHELF by ANTARES_POLICY the way the store comes off
store_shelf(), an unknown name fatal at startup, and /q/health reports
the engine and its timeout.

The gate belongs to the operation and is taken where the request enters
its handler: the shared query engines below it never gate, because one
operation runs them many times — the EntityMap recheck walks candidates
in chunks, build_temporal_map re-enters the temporal query, and the
snapshot fill pages through it under a header map that is not the
client's. tests/policy_gate_seam.rs reads the route list out of
router()'s own source and drives all 68 method/path pairs against a
counting engine, so a handler added without a gate is a red test.

The walk found two holes: update_registration carried a second gate
claiming 5.9.4, which is Delete Context Source Registration, while
delete_registration had none.

Each gate is one line through a gate! macro at the crate root: the
eight-line call it replaces was the same eight lines 53 times, and
dev/dup-check.sh read that as 14 new clone groups over the ratchet.

subscriptions.last_commit_message:
fix(chart): the time-axis drag emits zoom like every other viewport move

Dragging the time axis stretches the bars, which changes the visible window,
and it was the one gesture that did it silently: the plot drag, its kinetic
glide, the wheel, a pinch, a double-click and the keyboard commands all
announce themselves. A host sizing itself off `chart.on('zoom')` therefore
kept rendering for a window it no longer had, which is how our footprint
went on writing digits into columns an axis drag had squeezed to 5 px.

It goes through `_emitViewportIfMoved`, not a bare emit, so bar spacing
clamped at its limit stays silent under the same rule as every other path,
and the pan/zoom choice is made by whether the span moved.

`restoreState` had the same hole from the other side: it applied a saved
`barSpacing` directly to the time scale and only the saved `viewport` half
went through an emitting setter, so a state carrying spacing alone moved the
window without a word. The two are now bracketed and announced once, so a
restore is one event to a listener rather than none or two.

Docs and the skills reference pick both up. Base engine 61.91 -> 61.94 KB,
package 126.50 -> 126.53 KB.

He asked what we need FMP for — and the answer is nothing; yfinance already returns the forward leg

Operator, on the #333 block: "what do we need it for? we already have lots of

position, and he is right that the fork I put to him was the wrong one.

WHAT OUR EXISTING SOURCES ACTUALLY GIVE. Polygon is used here for news, splits
and tickers, and its /vX/reference/financials is REPORTED financials from
filings — backward-looking, which is the trailing leg the rubric already scores.
Alpaca is price and trading. Neither sells consensus FORWARD estimates, and the
forward leg is the only thing this task needs.

BUT YFINANCE DOES, AND IT IS ALREADY A DEPENDENCY AT $0. Verified live tonight:
revenue_estimate and earnings_estimate return avg / low / high /
numberOfAnalysts / yearAgoRevenue / growth per period. That maps one-for-one
onto the raw fields this recorder was built to store, and numberOfAnalysts is
exactly what the n_analysts < 3 -> None rule needs.

THE ONE REAL LIMITATION, stated rather than buried: the horizon is 0q / +1q /
0y / +1y — two forward quarters plus two forward years, not the >=4 forward
QUARTERS Pradeep durability asks for. The +1y annual is a coarser proxy for the
further-out leg. Whether that is enough for the axis is a methodology question,
and it is a far smaller one than a subscription. yfinance is also
unofficial/scraped, which is a reliability risk — and precisely why this
recorder stores a daily point-in-time snapshot instead of trusting one read.

So #333 goes blocked -> pending: no money decision, no new vendor. The work is a
scoped swap of one call. The SEC EDGAR anchor, the honest-window stamping, the
no-abort shape and the secret redaction all stand and were verified live tonight.

I had written the fork as "pay, switch source, or drop the axis" without first
checking what we already had. That is the shape of "don't defend the status quo

fix(s3): sign read URLs the way the bucket actually addresses objects

Attachments stored on COS could be uploaded but never downloaded. The
receiver only ever showed an image placeholder, and nothing in the chain
logged an error.

Two defects, both in the read path. operator_for_source hardcoded region
"auto" and never enabled virtual-host addressing, so presigned reads came
out path-style. Tencent COS forbids path-style: measured on one object,
virtual-hosted returns 200 and path-style returns 403. The upload side
(s3_backend) has honoured addressing_style all along; the read side did
not, which is why uploads looked healthy.

The second is the prefix. The S3 direct path stores the full object key,
path_prefix included, while the operator's root is that same prefix, so
presigning the stored value asked for prefix/prefix/... The proxy path
stores the key without the prefix, so the read side has to accept both;
storage_relative_path strips it when present.

Verified end to end against the production COS bucket: image sent from
one simulator, sealed object lands under the test prefix at exactly
36 + 32*chunks + plaintext bytes, and the receiver downloads and renders
it.

subscriptions.name: kythira
subscriptions.last_commit_message:
build: serialise the four 5.6 GiB HTTP-transport TUs with a Ninja job pool

Root-cause fix for the stdexec full-suite leg, which failed six times
across three PRs in a day -- as `exit 143` (the platform reclaiming an
over-memory VM) and as an 82-minute stall into the 180-minute timeout.
No compiler error was ever involved: the job logs contain zero `error:`
lines.

Instrumenting the CI build found it. Sampling every 30 s, the leg runs at

    mem_used 15,879 MiB    mem_available 109 MiB    swap_used 19,185 MiB

sustained for ~90 minutes -- a ~35 GiB footprint on a 16 GiB runner --
with only three compilers alive. The peak coincides with four
translation units: three_way_http_transport_equivalence_test,
http_implementation_interop_test, proxygen_transport_test and
proxygen_negotiation_integration_test.

Measured individually under this backend:

    three_way_http_transport_equivalence_test   5,649 MiB   <- one TU
    proxygen_transport_example                  2,274 MiB
    grpc_transport_integration_test             1,600 MiB
    11 docker_chaos TUs together at -j4           648 MiB
    linking all 19 docker_chaos binaries           35 MiB

Each compiles cleanly alone. Three at 5.6 GiB do not fit in 15 GiB, and
that is the entire failure. Each of these TUs instantiates the Beast,
Proxygen and cpp-httplib stacks together, and stdexec's sender types
multiply what that costs.

A job pool of 1 serialises exactly these four while every other target
stays parallel. Validated on PR #307, carrying this change on top of
#298's exact failing content: all legs green, and the leg finished in
1 h 53 m against 2 h 27 m and 2 h 33 m for the two -j3 runs before it.
Faster, not slower -- removing the swapping recovers far more wall clock
than the lost parallelism costs.

Also corrects the -j3 comment added in d7dd1e3, which was wrong. It
cited 2.27 GiB as the heaviest TU and argued 4 x 2.27 overran the runner
while 3 x 2.27 did not. The real figure is 5.6 GiB, in a TU that had not
been measured when that comment was written, and -j3 did not fix the
leg. The comment now says so and points at this pool as the actual fix.
-j3 itself is left in place because it is the configuration the green
validation run used; whether -j$(nproc) is now safe is a separate
experiment to run on evidence.

subscriptions.name: Budget
subscriptions.last_commit_message:
fix(repair): duplicate cleanup cascades, and always keeps one half of a pair

Two problems in the same loop, both found while wiring the cascade.

The delete went straight to the mapper, so splits, tags, attachments
and expense shares on a removed transaction were orphaned: no foreign
keys hold them, and every cleanup query - deleteAll, which factory
reset uses - finds its rows by joining back through
budget_transactions, so an orphan survives even that (#359). It now
goes through TransactionService::deleteAsAccountOwner(), which
cascades and resolves the account owner, since a duplicate can sit in
a shared account (#334).

The second is worse. Three detectors flag the same rows and each
picks its own keeper: the created_at grouping keeps the earliest
dated row, the same-bill-in-a-month pass keeps the latest created -
and two placeholders written by one markPaid share a created_at, so
that comes down to sort order. A pair flagged both ways therefore had
BOTH halves deleted, taking the payment along with the duplicate. The
loop now never deletes a row another finding is keeping, and skips a
finding whose original is itself going rather than guessing; what is
left over is picked up on a second run.

The existing test masked it by mocking findById to return null for
the other half, so only one delete ever happened under test.

subscriptions.last_commit_message:
api: q, mine, since and until filters on GET /v1/jobs (#178)

* docs: add web2-jb spec (jobs list q, mine, since, until backend)

Lane JB of the 2026-09-02 web-frontend batch: the backend halves of the
job search box, the My jobs toggle and the Timeline view's time window.
Four optional predicates threaded through the 15 existing jobs list and
count statements via sqlc.narg, composing with sort (the sort-versus-filter
400 is a guard over the two hard-coded ORDER BY statements, not a rule
about filters), strpos over escaped ILIKE, a half-open created_at window,
one owner composite index. Refuted: the mine item's cited workers
precedent is a constant predicate, not a parameterized one; the timeline
item's claim that a window needs no pagination.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs: add web2-jb plan (jobs list q, mine, since, until backend)

Ten TDD tasks: migration 000023, the 15 statement edits with the nine
sort variants re-parenthesised (their cursor guard is an unparenthesised
OR, so an appended AND filter would be ignored on every first page),
parseJobFilters as the single producer, handler wiring, the arm guard
derived from JobsSortSpec.Keys, the remaining properties, a CLI live
--status test, the EXPLAIN capture, README, and gates. Refuted the spec's
claim that no CLI integration test drives jobs list: four already do, so
the gap is narrowed to --status against a live server.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* store: migration 000023 adds idx_jobs_submitted_created_id

Serves GET /v1/jobs?mine=true under the default sort and its count, in the
same shape as idx_sched_jobs_owner_created. Plain CREATE INDEX because
golang-migrate wraps each migration in a transaction.

The guard asserts the indexdef fragment, not just the name, and the down
test carries a positive control so a green cannot come from the index never
having existed.

RED observed before the migration existed: the exists test failed at
require.NoError with "no rows in result set" and the down test failed at its
positive control with "fixture: idx_jobs_submitted_created_id must exist
before the down migration".

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* store,api: thread four optional filter predicates through the jobs list and count statements

q (substring over job name and owner email), owner_id, since and until are
appended as sqlc.narg predicates to the twelve list statements and the three
count statements. No statement is added. CountJobs and CountJobsByStatus
acquire the users join the list statements already have; it is total
(jobs.submitted_by is NOT NULL REFERENCES users) so it cannot change a count.

The nine suffixed sort variants wrote their cursor guard unparenthesised
(WHERE NOT cursor_set OR keyset). Appending AND (filter) to that binds as
(NOT cursor_set) OR (keyset AND filter), so every first page would have
ignored all four filters with no error. The disjunction is now wrapped.

strpos rather than escaped ILIKE so % and _ stay literal with nothing to
escape and nothing to miscopy. The cost is recorded where the predicate
lives: a trigram index can never serve strpos.

The regenerated Params types came out as the plan predicted - Q *string,
OwnerID pgtype.UUID, Since and Until pgtype.Timestamptz - though sqlc placed
PageLimit after the four rather than before them, which named struct
literals do not care about.

Behaviour is unchanged by this commit - every call site spreads an
explicitly-absent jobFilters. TestListJobs_Sort_OrderingAcrossKeys and
TestListJobs_Sort_PaginationAcrossPages pass on all ten arms, which is what
proves the re-parenthesisation left the keyset intact, and the existing jobs
list, sort, pagination and enrichment tests pass with a zero-line test diff.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* api: parseJobFilters, the single producer for q/mine/since/until

One place reads the four parameters, validates them and produces the
store-typed values; every call site spreads that one struct. Validation is
strict rather than lenient in the style of ?force=: ?force=garbage fails
toward the gentler action, while a misread filter renders a list that is
wrong and looks authoritative.

Each parameter is read via Query()[name] so a repeated parameter is a 400
rather than a silent first-wins, following the ?task= precedent on the retry
endpoint. UTF-8 is validated before the value can reach Postgres as a text
parameter, so user input cannot produce a 5xx. mine=true resolves the owner
from the context user and fails closed with 401 when there is none.

Every error body in the contract is pinned by a test, and the q length cap
is proved to be in runes by a pair of inputs a byte cap would classify the
other way round. The plan's listing for that test spelled the discriminating
rune as a raw literal and described it as three bytes; U+00E9 is two bytes
in UTF-8, and the test now asserts the 400-byte fixture length directly. The
rune is written as a \u escape so the source file stays pure ASCII - a raw
non-ASCII byte here survives every check this repo runs.

RED observed: the test file failed to build with "undefined: parseJobFilters".

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* api: honour q/mine/since/until on every GET /v1/jobs branch

handleListJobs reads the four parameters once, through parseJobFilters, and
the values reach the scheduled-job branch, the status branch and all ten sort
arms plus their three counts. They are parsed after the sort-versus-filter
guard so that rule's 400 keeps its precedence, and they are not added to
hasFilter: they are threaded into every sort variant and never touch ORDER
BY, so they cannot create the ordering gap that guard exists to close.

The test asserts that two users issuing byte-identical requests get disjoint
lists, with an unfiltered control on the same token so the disjointness
cannot come from the seeding.

RED observed before the wiring: both tokens saw [bob-job alice-job] where
one row was wanted, and both totals read 2.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* api: arm-enumerating guard for the four jobs-list filters

Option A's failure mode is a forgotten Params field on exactly one arm: a
zero value that silently disables one filter for one ordering. The guard is
behavioural rather than structural - it asserts what the endpoint returns -
and its arm table is derived from JobsSortSpec.Keys rather than hand-listed,
so a sort key added later without its predicates turns this red. 108
subtests, 12 arms crossed with 9 filters.

Two mutations were sequenced against it and both were killed narrowly.

Deleting the four filter fields from the priority-ascending arm alone
reddens exactly its nine sort=priority subtests and nothing else: 9 failed,
99 passed.

Dropping the parentheses this lane added around the ByNameDesc cursor guard,
so the WHERE parses as (NOT cursor_set) OR (keyset AND filter) again, reddens
exactly the nine sort=-name subtests: 9 failed, 99 passed. Each reports both
fixture rows where one was wanted, which is the silent-first-page shape the
re-parenthesisation exists to prevent. Both files were restored by editing
back and confirmed byte-identical by checksum, never by git checkout.

The fixture's two rows differ on all four axes independently: q=% and q=_
each select one row under strpos and BOTH rows under an unescaped ILIKE, and
the since/until bounds are the rows' own created_at values so the half-open
interval is pinned by rows sitting exactly on each bound. A companion test
asserts the unfiltered request returns both rows on every arm, so no
assertion above can be satisfied vacuously.

Two deviations from the plan's listing, both narrowing it. The unread
aliceMail fixture field is dropped rather than carried. uuidText is not
declared: package api_test already has uuidString for exactly this, and
redeclaring an equivalent helper is the drift the plan's own do-not-redeclare
rule is aimed at.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* api: half-open window, filtered total, and cursor-independent filter correctness

Three properties the arm-enumerating guard does not reach:

  * [since, until) is half-open, pinned by rows sitting exactly on each bound
    so a slip at either end changes the answer, and until == since is a legal
    empty window rather than a 400. Measured: changing >= to > on the base
    statement's since predicate drops the at-since row and reddens the test,
    reporting [inside] where [at-since inside] was wanted. The statement was
    restored by editing back and confirmed byte-identical by checksum.
  * total counts rows matching every active predicate, independent of the
    cursor. limit=1 separates a correct total from one echoing the page size
    and from one counting the unfiltered table, and an unfiltered control
    reads the table size on the same fixture.
  * a cursor carries no filter fingerprint and the server does not reject a
    mismatched one, so the defined safe failure mode is asserted directly: a
    stale cursor may move the starting position but can never return a row
    failing the current predicate. The page is asserted non-empty so that
    claim is not vacuous.

All four passed on their first run, which is expected - Tasks 2 to 4 already
implement what they describe. They are acceptance criteria 4, 6 and 7, and
the mutation above is what establishes the first is not vacuous rather than
a manufactured RED against production code.

The whole internal/api integration package is green at 9m28s, which is why
the lane runs at -timeout 1800s.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* cli: pin jobs list --status against a live server

The CLI's list command sends only status and sort, and none of the four new
parameters, so this lane cannot break it - but that was an argument and this
is the evidence. The bare list path already had live coverage in this
package; --status did not, and it is the only CLI path reaching the status
branch whose statement gained four predicates and whose count moved from a
bare string argument to a Params struct. The empty case is asserted too so a
total that stopped being the filtered count cannot pass on rendered rows
alone.

This is the narrower true claim. The spec said the CLI real-server lane has
no coverage for jobs list at all; internal/cli/jobs_integration_test.go
already drives doListJobs against the live harness in four tests, so the gap
was --status specifically, not the endpoint.

No production change to internal/cli.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs: document the four jobs-list filters, and correct the Filter + sort paragraph

Three edits. The endpoint table row names the four new parameters and links
to the new subsection. The subsection gives the formats, the half-open
window, every exact 400 body, the composition rules, and the requirement to
drop the cursor when a filter changes.

The third edit is the one that matters most: the Filter + sort paragraph
stayed true the moment four composable filters existed, and became
misleading. A reader who infers 'filters exclude sort' from it writes a
frontend that never combines search with sorting. It now says explicitly
which two parameters the rejection is scoped to and why, and that the four
new ones compose with ?sort=.

44 insertions and 2 deletions, proportionate to the two replaced lines plus
a 42-line subsection. Every added byte is ASCII and the file still decodes
as UTF-8.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* api: reject a NUL byte in ?q= instead of 500ing

GET /v1/jobs?q=%00 and ?q=abc%00 returned 500. Postgres text cannot hold a
NUL byte and rejects one with SQLSTATE 22021, and utf8.ValidString does not

* store: drop migration 000023; the mine=true list never uses that index

reaches a generic plan, then EXPLAIN ANALYZEd on the seventh:

  plan_cache_mode=auto,               list  uses idx_jobs_submitted_created_id = false
  plan_cache_mode=auto,               count uses idx_jobs_submitted_created_id = true
  plan_cache_mode=force_generic_plan, list  uses idx_jobs_submitted_created_id = false
  plan_cache_mode=force_generic_plan, count uses idx_jobs_submitted_created_id = false

The default-sort list statement under auto:

  Limit  (actual time=0.021..3.280 rows=51 loops=1)
    ->  Index Scan using idx_jobs_created_id on jobs j  (actual time=0.009..3.179 rows=51)
          Filter: ((($5 IS NULL) OR (submitted_by = $5)) AND (($6 IS NULL) OR ...))
          Rows Removed by Filter: 15153
  Execution Time: 3.304 ms

a placeholder rather than a literal, so the planner walks the ordering index
and filters. The count reaches the index only on a custom plan, which is the
first five executions of a connection's prepared statement and not the
steady state.

benefit: it is written on every job insert and update, and it makes a claim
in the schema that the plans contradict. Removing it, its down migration and
its guard test.

wraps each migration in a transaction, and the pgx5 driver runs each statement
with a bare Exec and no BEGIN, serializing with an advisory lock instead. That
claim dies with the file.

mine=true statement rather than an optional predicate. That is the

feat(import): QuickBooks Export-data ZIP imports the whole company [skip ci]

Tested against a real QBO "Export data" ZIP (Industrial Insight Inc, 10,220
transactions, 2016–2026) plus its Chart of accounts CSV. Before this the
import produced 1,993 transactions and 27,293 "does not balance" errors.

Sheet classification
- The Export-data General Ledger uses Debit/Credit/Balance columns (not
  Split/Amount), so it looked like a Journal and, sorting before "Journal",
  shadowed the real one. A Balance column now rejects Journal detection,
  qbo-gl reads the Debit/Credit layout and the per-row Account column, and
  selectSourceSheets prefers the sheet named Journal.
- Balance Sheet / Profit and Loss / Customers / Vendors / Employees sheets
  are recognised and used.

Account tree (qbo-tree.ts)
- The Chart of accounts CSV drives the book: GnuCash top-level placeholders
  (Assets, Liabilities, Equity, Income, Expenses), a group per QBO account
  type beneath them, every chart row nested under its group with the
  account_type coerced from the group, deleted journal-only accounts slotted
  by suffix-strip → chart parent → resolved type. Without the CSV, types
  fall back to the Balance Sheet + P&L sections (qbo-statements.ts).

Business records (qbo-business.ts)
- Customers, vendors and employees from the contact-list sheets, with
  ownership rows.
- Invoice / Credit Memo / Bill transactions become posted invoices and bills
  on the journal transaction itself: entries per line, an A/R–A/P lot, the
  gncInvoice posting slots. Payments apply FIFO per owner with the A/R–A/P
  split divided across lots; QBO's zero-amount credit-link payments apply
  credit notes; prepayments settle later-dated documents.

Result on the real export: 227 accounts, 10,220 transactions, 112/491/19
contacts, 908 invoices + 5 credit notes + 81 bills, 959 paid in full, totals
tie to the QBO general ledger to the cent.

subscriptions.last_commit_message:
the grid's GIOP gap was two causes, and neither was coverage

Ranked as "coverage, not transparency". Working it found otherwise, twice.

PYTHON'S MISSING 1.1 WAS NOT A FACT ABOUT PYTHON. The two client-jacorb.sh
cells disagreed — Java read `1.1 1.2`, Python read `1.2` — because Java's cell
had a per-version loop and Python's had none. The suite's `neither` column
carried that as though Python could not reach the other versions. AXES states
the rule it broke: the suite is one suite, parameterised by language, never a
copy. The loop is spikes/lib/giop_versions.sh now and both cells call it; the
only language-specific part of a version pass is which driver runs, which is
the callback.

CONTROL for the lift: Java's readings are unchanged — 2 order/version readings,
the same 1.0 note with the same reason, the same 12 completed calls — and
Python's client went read[1.2] -> read[1.1 1.2].

AND THE LIFT IMMEDIATELY REPRODUCED A DEFECT ALREADY WRITTEN DOWN HERE. The
shared function restated the Java cell's looser reason-extraction pattern
instead of lifting the corrected one from client-omniorb.sh, so Python's 1.0
note came out carrying

  raise TransportError(reply["error"].get("message", ...))

a traceback SOURCE line where the reason belongs — the exact defect that file's
comment records fixing. A shared function that restates one caller's assumption
is a copy with a library's manners. Fixed by lifting the pattern, not rewriting
it; both cells now report the exception line.

GIOP 1.0 IS NOT A FIXTURE LIMITATION, and the note that said so was half the
story. Both drivers gained `--no-wide` (off by default, so every other cell
drives exactly what it drove) and 1.0 STILL DID NOT OPEN:
orbweaver_dynamic::invoke calls wide_codec(conn) unconditionally before
marshalling anything (invoke.rs:129), so EVERY call on a GIOP 1.0 connection is
refused, ping() included — measured as zero completed cases before the first
failure, and readable as an unconditional `?` two lines after the signature is
in hand. §9.3.1.6 forbids carrying wchar/wstring DATA; it does not forbid a
`long ping()`. A peer that speaks only GIOP 1.0 cannot be called at all.

wide_codec's own doc comment names the better behaviour — "saying so at that
point is more useful than refusing every call on a 1.0 connection — but the
invoker cannot know yet" — and the invoker CAN know.

NOT FIXED HERE, deliberately. That is the core invoke path every binding uses,
and folding it into suite plumbing would be work that is correct apart and wrong
together (D028). It is its own batch, and both plan documents now say so where
they used to call this item coverage.

Harness 93: exit 0, all measured checks green, 6 counted SKIPPED.

Phase 97: the pointer nobody followed

Phase 96 gave the losing record a merged_into_id and claimed in its ADR that
this meant "a bookmark, an export or somebody's memory of the old name still
lands somewhere that explains itself". That was false when written. grep
finds one use of the column in the whole application and it is the set that
writes it. What somebody actually found was an archived customer with no
documents and no explanation — worse than before the merge, when it at least
had its invoices.

The correction is written into ADR 0096 rather than the sentence quietly
edited away, on Phase 91's reasoning: a wrong reason written down is more
dangerous than none, because the next person builds on it. The claim
described an intention as though it were behaviour.

An archive and a merge are different acts and now say so. The row reads
"merged into Cascade Joinery" where there is a pointer and "archived" where
there is not, naming the survivor so nobody is left knowing something
happened and not where to look. The name comes from a correlated subquery
rather than a self-join, for the reason Phase 92 gave: a join can multiply
rows, and a list that silently doubled a customer would be worse than the
defect being fixed.

Evidence of what moved belongs on the act, not on each thing moved. The
merge takes its ids from returning "id" on the update itself, so there is no
second query whose answer could differ from what was written, and records
them on the event — the trail can now answer "did this invoice move" rather
than only "five invoices moved". An audit row per document was rejected:
hundreds of rows saying the same thing on the same day would bury every
other entry in both histories. The ids are capped at 500 with the cap
recorded as its own truncated field rather than inferred from the list
length, which is wrong for a merge of exactly 500.

An event may write a sentence about itself. The merge entry read "Records
merged" and named nothing, above "Role nothing → absorbed" — the payload
describing its own filing. Told gains a summary, written where the facts are
known rather than reconstructed from an action name, and role/side/summary
join reason in NOT_A_CHANGE. Also fixed: party.merge was in the correction
vocabulary and not in the audit story, so the one screen that would explain
a merge showed the raw action code.

subscriptions.last_commit_message: Require a token for the one AJAX action that changes state Opening the notification bell marked every notification read, and it did so with a bare GET carrying no session token. Another site could fire the same request with nothing more than an tag pointing at it, and the browser would attach the user's cookies. The damage is small -- somebody else's notifications get marked read -- but a state change over an unauthenticated GET is the shape of the problem, not its size, and the report's security chapter claims a token on every state-changing request. mark_read now requires POST and a valid token. The token reaches the script the same way BASE_URL already does, from the footer; same-origin policy is what keeps it out of another site's reach, since a third party cannot read this page's body to lift it. The read-only actions, count and list, stay plain GETs. They change nothing and are already scoped to the session's own user_id, so a forged request could only ask the server to tell the user something about themselves. subscriptions.last_commit_message:
M1: FHIRPath lexer and parser

First half of the FHIRPath engine. Everything the server does with resource
contents is expressed in FHIRPath -- search extraction, invariants, _filter,
subscription criteria -- so this package is built and proven before anything
depends on it.

Parsing is separated from evaluation because the conformance index holds
thousands of expressions that are compiled once and reused; re-parsing them
per resource would dominate indexing cost.

Two design notes
  - No keyword token kinds. Words like "div", "and", and "contains" are
    operators in one position and ordinary property names in another --
    "Patient.contains" is a valid path -- so the lexer emits every bare word
    as an identifier and the parser decides by position. This is why the
    parser matches operators on identifier text rather than token kind.
  - Precedence is spelled out as an explicit ladder rather than a table.
    Getting it wrong silently changes the meaning of real expressions instead
    of failing, so it is written to be read against the grammar.

Proven against the specification's own expressions, not hand-written ones:
the compiled indexes carry 4636 published expressions (every search parameter,
composite component, and invariant across R4 and R5). All 4636 parse, and all
render back to source that reparses identically -- a grouping bug generally
shows up as a round-trip mismatch.

One deliberate deviation from the grammar. FHIRPath delimits strings with
single quotes only, and the official test suite never uses double quotes as
delimiters. R5's ElementDefinition eld-11 invariant is nonetheless written
type.code.contains(":"). It is the only such expression in either release,
and reference implementations tolerate it, which is why the slip survived
publication. Rejecting it would mean refusing to evaluate a real invariant
and quietly weakening StructureDefinition validation, so it is accepted as
a string literal. Pinned by a named test so it reads as a decision rather
than an oversight.

Parse of a representative search expression: ~4.9us, 30 allocs.

Let a new daily habit make an hour busy before the month notices

Thirty days is a steady state, and a routine can change overnight.

Three consecutive weekday mornings departed in the 07:00 hour — trips
492, 498 and 500, at 07:21, 07:26 and 07:28 — while the thirty-day
histogram still rated that hour at 2 departures against the 06:00
hour's 13, because it was counting a routine that had already ended.
Trip 500 came out 72% blind and 28% high on Wh/km, and scraped under the
share that would have blanked its energy entirely by three points. At
one departure a weekday that hour needs two to three WEEKS to cross the
ordinary threshold, and every morning until then costs the same.

I dismissed this hour yesterday on the strength of that histogram, which
is the mistake the second rule exists to stop: reading a median over a
month as evidence about this week.

So an hour is also busy with departures on three of the last seven days.
Distinct DAYS, not departures, because the question is whether something
happens daily — three trips in one afternoon is an errand, three
mornings running is a habit. Three of seven catches the habit and leaves
the midday hours alone: on this car those run about two days in seven
each, and tightening all of them would cost ten times what tightening
the one that matters does.

subscriptions.last_commit_message:
local-webhook 0.27.0: a CI event's meta carries the commit it reports on (#54)

One failing run reaches a standing watch as up to six event shapes —
workflow_run, workflow_job, check_run, check_suite, a bare commit status
and deployment_status — and a spawn command that wants to react ONCE has
to recognise them as one thing. Nothing in the meta let it.

The routing key cannot: every run in the repo shares it. The run id
cannot either — check_run, check_suite and status do not carry one. The
commit can: every shape names the sha it is reporting on, at a path of
its own, so the sha is the only field that links the shapes. It now goes
in the meta, and `branch` rides along where the payload has one.

Measured cost of not having it, agent-box#510/#511: the deploy-test
failure on that box's master arrived as workflow_run and then, 63 s
later, as check_run. The window had closed, the coalescing brake ran and
found no owner — because the session spawned for the first shape can
only claim what the meta lets it name, and that was "this repo's CI".
Claiming the whole repo swallowed a red master once already
(agent-box#384), so agent-box had narrowed the claim to topic branches,
which leaves a shared ref claiming nothing at all. Two sessions
investigated the same run and filed the same issue twice, neither
knowing about the other.

With a sha in the meta the consumer claims the run in front of it, which
is the right width in both directions: a second shape of the SAME run
reaches the session already on it, and a LATER red master is a different
commit, so it still gets a session of its own.

Deliberately not a run id, and `branch` is not identity: two runs on one
branch are two runs. A bare commit status carries only a `branches`
list, which the predicate walker cannot index (local-channels#46), so
that shape gets a sha and no branch — and is claimable all the same,
which no branch-shaped claim could manage.

agent-box pins this repo by revision, so the companion change that
actually writes the narrower claim goes in that repo's
webhook-spawn.sh with the pin bump.

Refs: agent-box#510, agent-box#511, agent-box#384, #46

subscriptions.name: FlightRadar
subscriptions.last_commit_message:
Draw trails from the smoothed position, not the raw fix

A trail should be the record of where the blip actually went. It was being
pushed from applyUpdate straight off the incoming fix, while the blip itself
is drawn from a position that chases that fix with SMOOTH_TAU easing. So the
blip glided through every correction and the trail took the same correction
as a hard vertex -- a visibly kinked path behind an aircraft that looked
like it was flying smoothly.

That is not rare. Position squitters are dropped long before an aircraft
stops being heard: sampled over 60s, a contact at -23dBFS got a fresh
position on only 7 of 20 polls with a worst gap of 18.7s, and one at -26dBFS
managed a single fix in 51 seconds. Dead reckoning carries the blip straight
ahead through each gap, so every one of them ends in a correction when the
real fix lands.

Now sampled from the render loop at 4Hz off the eased position, which makes
the trail the history of the drawn path and therefore smooth by
construction. On the same 18s-gap-then-turn case the correction spreads over
seven decaying segments (12, 13, 6, 3, 1.2, 0.6, 0.5 px) instead of one jump.

Points are skipped when the blip has not moved ~0.02nm since the last
sample, which is under half a pixel at this scale. Without that, an aircraft
whose eased position had converged recorded a duplicate four times a second
-- 23 coincident points in six seconds in testing, now 1.

Cost measured against live traffic: 6 aircraft, 1741 trail points, longest
track 614 points. drawTrails went from 0.05ms to 0.228ms, and the whole
canvas render is 0.9% of the 15fps frame budget.
